nature-econ-398.title: Concentration ratios: how much the biggest firms hold
nature-econ-398.text: Add up the market shares of the largest few firms in a market, such as the top four, and you have a concentration ratio. The four-firm ratio is 100 per cent for a monopoly and zero for perfect competition. Studies suggest a ratio between 40 and 70 percent points to an oligopoly. Concentration measures are the most common gauge of market power, because they need only revenue data, though they ignore costs and profits.

nature-econ-366.title: The Walrasian auction: finding prices by bidding
nature-econ-366.text: A Walrasian auction finds a competitive equilibrium by steadily raising prices. The auctioneer starts all prices at zero, and at each round buyers name their favorite bundle. Any item wanted by more than one buyer has its price raised, until each item is wanted by at most one buyer. Such mechanisms are also called Walrasian tâtonnement, or English versions of {{ref:nature-econ-671}}.

nature-econ-384.title: The Herfindahl index: weighing market concentration
nature-econ-384.text: Square every firm's market share and add them up: the result is the Herfindahl index, a measure of how concentrated a market is. Squaring gives big firms more weight than a simple concentration ratio does. The index runs from 1/N to 1, where N is the number of firms. The more concentrated the market, the higher the value.

nature-econ-375.title: Excess supply: more for sale than buyers want
nature-econ-375.text: If 1000 televisions are offered at $600 but buyers want only 300, the 700 left over push sellers to cut the price until the market balances. That leftover is excess supply, also called a market surplus or glut. Sellers want to sell more than buyers want to buy, because the price sits above its equilibrium level. It is the opposite of a shortage, and the two are the two kinds of disequilibrium in a competitive market. Unemployment is excess supply in the labor market. Farmers face it after a good harvest, and governments may step in to buy up the perishable surplus.

nature-econ-405.title: Price floors: a legal minimum price
nature-econ-405.text: Before US airfares were deregulated in 1978, price floors kept flying so costly that in 1965 more than 80% of Americans had never flown on a jet. A price floor is a limit, set by government or another body, on the lowest price that may be charged for a product or service. It only bites if it is set above the equilibrium price; set below, it has no practical effect. Common examples are laws setting the lowest legal wage, supply management in Canadian farming, US airfares before 1978 and minimum prices for alcohol. A binding floor makes buyers buy less while sellers want to sell more, leaving a lasting surplus. It shifts some of the buyers' gains to producers and creates a pure loss to society ({{ref:nature-econ-345}}). EU support buying to hold farm prices at an intervention price has sometimes left "butter mountains" of surplus in warehouses. Floors can also steady a market. Hybrid cap-and-trade schemes add floor and ceiling prices to steady the carbon price.

nature-econ-376.title: Factor markets: buying land, labor and capital
nature-econ-376.text: Firms sell what they make in product markets, but they buy their inputs in factor markets, where land, labor and capital are bought and sold. Both kinds of market work in much the same way. Factor markets share out land, labor and capital among firms and pay income to their owners as wages, rents and the like. A factor in scarce supply earns a high price and an abundant one a low price, so when a factor's supply falls, its equilibrium price rises. Firms hire at the margin. A firm takes on another worker when the extra revenue that worker brings in exceeds the extra cost.

nature-econ-377.title: Monopsony: the market with one buyer
nature-econ-377.text: A monopsony is the buying-side mirror of a monopoly: a market with a single dominant buyer. An oligopsony has a few. Instead of taking the price of an input from the market, a monopsonist sets it, choosing a point on the input's supply curve. Monopsonies are more common in factor markets than in product markets, and there is growing concern about them in some kinds of labor.

nature-econ-372.title: Derived demand: wanting inputs because people want products
nature-econ-372.text: If shoppers want more new cars, carmakers want more of the inputs used to build them. That is derived demand: demand for an input that comes from demand for the final product it helps make. The link is direct and positive. A good used to make another, final good is called an intermediate good. Labor works the same way, and a firm's demand for it slopes downward: when the wage rises, the quantity of labor wanted falls.

nature-econ-393.title: The Lerner index: measuring the markup
nature-econ-393.text: Named after the economist Abba Lerner, the Lerner index measures market power as the gap between price and marginal cost, taken as a share of price. It runs from zero in a perfectly competitive market to 1. The closer to 1, the bigger the gap. At the profit-maximizing point, (P − MC)/P equals minus one over the elasticity of demand, so less elastic demand means a higher markup.

nature-econ-390.title: Veblen goods: when a high price is the point
nature-econ-390.text: Diamonds, gold, precious stones, famous paintings and antiques can become more wanted as they get dearer. These are Veblen goods: luxuries whose demand rises with their price, because a high price signals status. Thorstein Veblen described such buying as paying for status and social position rather than for extra usefulness.

nature-econ-406.title: The minimum wage: a price floor for labor
nature-econ-406.text: A minimum wage is a price floor for labor: the lowest hourly rate an employer is allowed by law to pay. Standard theory predicts trouble if it is set above the market wage for low-skilled work. Employers hire fewer workers, for example by switching to self-service or machines. The higher wage also draws more people into the labor market, producing a surplus of labor. Yet since the credibility revolution of the 1990s, minimum wages have often won strong support among economists, so the question remains contested.

nature-econ-396.title: The market mechanism: prices doing the sharing
nature-econ-396.text: Buyers and sellers exchanging money for goods, at prices that reflect value and scarcity, tend to share out goods and services well. That is the market mechanism. Its quality depends on information: prices tell producers what people want, and the less accurate that information, the worse the coordination and the fewer wants are met. The mechanism has limits. It often cannot provide shared goods ({{ref:nature-econ-633}}) well, because of problems such as the one in {{ref:nature-econ-606}}, so highways needed government planning. Free-market economies leave resources to the private sector, planned economies to the public sector, and mixed economies to both.

nature-econ-414.title: The zero-profit condition: competition erases profit
nature-econ-414.text: In gold rushes few prospectors got rich, but many people built successful businesses selling shovels. The zero-profit condition describes where competition leads: when firms can enter or leave an industry almost freely, each firm's economic profit is pushed to zero. If firms earn positive economic profit, newcomers join until it is gone. If they make losses, firms leave until profit rises back to zero. This settled state is called the industry's long run, and it is close to perfect competition. In neoclassical models, the condition also makes a market economy of profit-seeking firms compatible with zero growth.

nature-econ-338.title: Economic surplus: the gains from trading
nature-econ-338.text: Early writers used the idea of surplus to study food. Farming must feed everyone, so the rest of the economy is limited by the food farmers produce beyond their own needs. Today economic surplus means the total gain that buyers and sellers get from trading in a market. The engineer Jules Dupuit first put forward the idea in the mid-19th century, and the economist Alfred Marshall made it famous, so it is also called Marshallian surplus. It has two parts. The buyers' share, {{ref:nature-econ-339}}, is the area above the price and below the demand curve on a supply and demand diagram. The sellers' share, {{ref:nature-econ-340}}, is the area below the price and above the supply curve. Their sum is called social or total surplus, or total welfare. When inefficiency shrinks that total, the lost part is called {{ref:nature-econ-345}}.

nature-econ-345.title: Deadweight loss: value that nobody gets
nature-econ-345.text: Suppose a cleaning deal would create $40 of total surplus, and a $50 tax is imposed on it. The trade never happens. The government collects nothing, and the $40 simply vanishes. That vanished value is deadweight loss. It is the loss of society's welfare when a good is produced or consumed at a quantity where its benefit to society does not equal its cost. Unlike most losses, which are someone else's gain, it is regained by no one. Either goods are made that cost more than they are worth, or worthwhile goods are not made. Monopoly pricing is one cause. Suppose nails cost $0.10 to make and a monopolist charges $0.60. Buyers who value a nail between those prices are shut out, and their lost benefit is deadweight loss. A subsidy can do the reverse. A $0.03 subsidy lowers the price to $0.07, so people who value a nail below its true $0.10 cost buy it, which wastes resources. Externalities, taxes, and binding caps and floors on prices, such as a minimum wage, cause it too. The more elastic supply and demand are, the bigger the loss from a tax. It also grows with the square of the tax: doubling the tax multiplies the loss by 4.

nature-econ-381.title: Gains from trade: why exchange pays
nature-econ-381.text: Gains from trade are the net benefits people or economies get when they can trade more freely with each other. David Ricardo first clearly stated and proved comparative advantage in 1817, and it remains the basic explanation for where they come from. Technically, they are the rise in buyers' and sellers' combined surplus that comes from lower tariffs or freer trade. They come from specialization, the larger total output it allows, and selling one kind of output for other goods valued more highly. Prices do the steering. They draw labor and other inputs toward activities where they have a comparative advantage, that is, a low opportunity cost. Freer trade is not always best for everyone. A large economy may use taxes and subsidies to gain at other economies' expense, and market power can let some traders block other mutually beneficial trades.

nature-econ-339.title: Consumer surplus: the bargain buyers get
nature-econ-339.text: Drinking water usually carries a large consumer surplus, because people would pay very high prices for it to survive. Consumer surplus is the gap between the most a buyer would be willing to pay for something and the price they actually pay. The first few liters of water are worth the most, since they prevent death, so they hold more surplus than later liters. That points to the general source of the surplus. Buyers value each extra unit less than the last, yet pay the same market price for every unit. On a graph, consumer surplus is the area under the demand curve and above the price; with a straight-line demand curve it is a triangle. A rise in consumer surplus after a price change is read as a gain in welfare, a fall as a loss. When supply grows and the price falls, existing buyers gain on the units they already bought, and new buyers enter and gain too.

nature-econ-403.title: Price discrimination: different buyers, different prices
nature-econ-403.text: Student and senior discounts are a form of price discrimination. The same seller charges different buyers different prices for the same or nearly the same good, according to which group they seem to belong to. It works by exploiting differences in buyers' willingness to pay and in how sensitive they are to price. The aim is to raise profit by shifting consumer surplus to the seller. It needs market power; otherwise buyers would switch sellers or resell cheap units to those charged more. Economists sort it into three degrees, a scheme attributed to Pigou. In first-degree, or perfect, price discrimination each buyer pays their maximum, so the seller captures all consumer surplus. Second-degree discrimination varies price with the quantity bought, and third-degree charges different groups different prices. Drug-makers charge more in wealthier countries, and antiretroviral drugs cost far less in Africa, where sales would otherwise be very limited.

nature-econ-340.title: Producer surplus: the sellers' gain
nature-econ-340.text: Every seller has a lowest price they would accept. Producer surplus is the gain sellers get when the market price is higher than that. It is roughly equal to profit, since producers will not normally sell at a loss. On a graph it is the area below the market price line and above the supply curve. Higher market prices raise it, while higher production costs or lower prices shrink it, and taxes, subsidies, new technology and competition can shift it. Economists use it to judge how taxes, subsidies, price controls and trade policies affect producers.

nature-econ-341.title: The rule of one-half: a shortcut for surplus
nature-econ-341.text: When supply changes a little and the demand curve stays put, how much do buyers gain? The rule of one-half gives a quick estimate of the change in consumer surplus. With straight-line demand, the change is a trapezoid. Its height is the price change, and its middle width is the average of the quantities before and after.

nature-econ-346.title: Harberger's triangle: the shape of lost surplus
nature-econ-346.text: On a supply and demand graph, the deadweight loss from government intervention in an otherwise perfect market appears as a triangle. It is generally credited to Arnold Harberger. The interventions include price floors, caps, taxes, tariffs and quotas. A tax, for example, drives a wedge between what buyers pay and sellers receive, and the triangle's area is the surplus lost for good. The triangle also measures the loss when a government fails to step into a market with externalities. How much it matters is disputed. Martin Feldstein holds these losses can drag down long-run growth, while James Tobin argued their effect on the economy is small.

nature-econ-394.title: Market clearing: no surplus, no shortage
nature-econ-394.text: Shops discount leftover Christmas decorations after Christmas until shoppers buy the excess supply. That is market clearing in miniature. Market clearing is the process by which a price settles where the amount supplied equals the amount demanded, leaving neither a surplus nor a shortage. The price that does it is the market-clearing, or equilibrium, price. A price above it builds up unsold stock. A price below it leaves buyers short, sometimes unable to find the product at any price. Shocks set the process going. After an earthquake destroys homes, a housing shortage pushes prices up, builders build more, and supply rises until it meets the new demand. From about 1785 to 1935 most economists took market clearing for granted. Then the long mass unemployment of the Great Depression led Keynes and others to doubt it. Most economists now see continuous market clearing as unrealistic but useful for long-run analysis. They still disagree over whether prices adjust quickly enough for markets to clear. Some blame sticky prices; others blame unions or government policy.

nature-econ-410.title: Shortages: when buyers want more than there is
nature-econ-410.text: In the 1980s Soviet Union, prices fixed artificially low left people queuing for cars, apartments and clothing. That is a shortage: a situation in which people want to buy more of a product than is available at the going price, also called excess demand. It is the opposite of excess supply. In a simple market, excess demand pushes the price up until demand matches supply, so a shortage persists only when something stops the price rising. Then something other than price, such as first come first served or a lottery, decides who gets the good. Causes include legal caps on prices, bans on selling a product and suppliers choosing not to raise prices. Shortages bring black markets, queues and rationing, more demand for substitutes, and wasted time that lowers overall wealth. Economists and historians note that lasting shortages and famines have mostly been caused by war, price controls and repressive regimes rather than by having too many people.

nature-econ-400.title: Price ceilings: a legal maximum price
nature-econ-400.text: Venezuela's food price ceilings from 2003 caused shortages and hoarding. A price ceiling is a limit, set by government or another body, on the highest price that may be charged for a product or service. Governments set them to protect consumers from goods becoming too expensive. Set below the market equilibrium price, a ceiling leads to a shortage. It also misallocates what supply there is: ceilings on Helsinki's Hitas apartments cause queuing and mean flats do not go to those who value them most. Ceilings can even raise prices, by giving competing firms a shared target to collude on. US states with an 18 percent interest cap saw rates just below it. Economists generally agree that consumer price controls fail at their aims, and many advise against them. A minority disagree. Isabella Weber argues for price caps to fight sellers' inflation, and Paul Krugman became open to them.

nature-econ-401.title: Rent control: a ceiling on housing costs
nature-econ-401.text: Rent control is a price ceiling on housing rents. The US rent controls of the 1940s, brought in under Franklin D. Roosevelt's Office of Price Administration, played out as economic models predicted. They cut the supply of rental homes available to returning veterans. At the same time homeownership and homes for sale rose, likely because landlords turned rentals into homes for sale.

reviews.markets-prices-and-surplus: Markets use prices to pass information, and this chapter showed how. Demand slopes down, supply slopes up, and the price settles where the two meet, an equilibrium that shifts whenever tastes, costs or incomes change. Elasticity measures how strongly buyers and sellers respond, which decides who bears a tax and how far a firm can mark up its price. Perfect competition drives price down to marginal cost and makes economic surplus as large as it can be, while monopoly, price controls and taxes open a deadweight loss that no one regains. Yet an equilibrium is not automatically good: a food market can be in equilibrium while people starve, and with externalities, markets on their own produce too much pollution.
